chapter_summary:
Just as a photographer or cinematographer uses a physical camera to capture a scene, you, as a 3D artist, use virtual cameras in Maya to define what the viewer sees. Cameras are your window into the 3D world, allowing you to frame your subjects, establish perspective, and convey emotion. Maya provides default cameras (like `persp`, `top`, `front`, `side`) that are always present and cannot be deleted. These are excellent for general navigation and modeling tasks. However, for rendering final images or animations, you will almost always create **custom cameras**. Custom cameras offer complete control over their position, orientation, and optical properties, allowing you to craft specific shots without affecting your modeling views.

Creating a custom camera is straightforward: go to `Create > Cameras > Camera` or `Camera and Aim` or `Camera, Aim, and Up`. The `Camera and Aim` option is particularly useful as it creates a camera and a separate "aim" locator. The camera will always point at this aim locator, simplifying the process of directing the camera at a specific subject. Once created, you can navigate through your custom camera's view by selecting it in the Outliner and then going to `Panels > Look Through Selected`. This changes your current viewport to display what that specific camera sees. You can then use the standard viewport navigation tools (Alt + Left/Middle/Right mouse button) to move the camera as if you were holding it. Alternatively, you can move the camera node directly using the `Move`, `Rotate`, and `Scale` tools, and observe the changes in a separate `Render View` or another viewport looking through that camera.

The power of custom cameras lies in their extensive attributes, found in the Attribute Editor. The **Focal Length** attribute is perhaps the most impactful. It mimics the focal length of real-world camera lenses and directly affects the perspective distortion and field of view. A short focal length (e.g., 18mm) creates a wide-angle, distorted view, often used for dramatic effect or to capture expansive environments. A long focal length (e.g., 200mm) results in a telephoto, compressed perspective, making distant objects appear closer and flattening depth, often used for close-ups or wildlife photography. Experimenting with focal length is crucial for achieving different cinematic looks. Another important set of attributes relates to **Depth of Field (DOF)**. DOF controls which parts of your scene are in sharp focus and which are blurred. By enabling `Depth of Field` in the camera's `Arnold` (or other renderer) attributes and adjusting `Focus Distance` (the distance from the camera to the point you want in sharpest focus) and `Aperture Size` (how much blur is applied to out-of-focus areas), you can create beautiful, realistic photographic effects that draw attention to your subject.

Effective camera work isn't just about technical settings; it's also about **composition**. Think about the rule of thirds, leading lines, and negative space. How can you frame your subject to make it visually appealing and convey the intended message? For game development, cameras are critical for defining player perspective (first-person, third-person), cinematic cutscenes, and even UI elements. For example, a wide-angle lens might be used for an establishing shot of a game level, while a telephoto lens could be used for a dramatic close-up during a character's dialogue.

To manage multiple camera angles or specific compositions within a scene, Maya offers **Camera Bookmarks**. These allow you to save the exact position, rotation, and focal length of a camera at a particular moment. You can create a bookmark by selecting your camera, then going to `View > Bookmarks > Edit Bookmarks...` and clicking `New Bookmark`. This is incredibly useful for quickly jumping between different pre-set shots without manually repositioning your camera.

Finally, cameras are not static; they can be animated. Basic camera animation involves setting **keyframes** for its `Translate` (position) and `Rotate` (orientation) attributes over time. For instance, you could keyframe a camera to move from a wide shot to a close-up, or to orbit around a character. Select your camera, go to a specific frame on the `Time Slider`, adjust the camera's position/rotation, and then press `s` on your keyboard (or `Animate > Set Key`) to set a keyframe. Move to another frame, adjust the camera again, and set another keyframe. Maya will then interpolate the movement between these keyframes, creating smooth animation. The Graph Editor (`Windows > Animation Editors > Graph Editor`) provides precise control over these animation curves, allowing you to refine the timing and easing of your camera movements. Mastering camera animation is essential for creating dynamic and engaging cinematic sequences.

narration.text: Cameras are the window you use to show your 3D work. In Maya you start with default cameras for modeling and navigation, but for final images and animation you create custom cameras that behave like a physical lens. In this lesson you'll learn how to make a Camera and Aim setup, how focal length changes perspective, how depth of field draws attention, and how to save and recall shots with bookmarks. You'll also see the basic workflow for animating a camera with keyframes so your shots can move smoothly. For example, creating a Camera and Aim gives you a separate aim locator so the camera always points at a specific subject without complex rotations. Understanding focal length — a short value for wide-angle distortion or a long value for telephoto compression — is essential to express scale and mood. Depth of field uses focus distance and aperture size to place sharpness where you want it and blur the rest. Finally, bookmarks and simple keyframes let you jump between planned shots and craft motion. As you go through this lesson, notice how technical settings and composition choices combine to tell a visual story. Think of a short scene you want to shoot and how each camera choice will change what the audience feels.

keyIdea.title: Why cameras matter
keyIdea.text: Custom Maya cameras let you control framing, lens characteristics, and motion so your 3D scenes read like intentional photographs or film shots.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish between Maya's always-present default cameras and the custom cameras you create for rendering. You will confidently create a Camera and Aim setup and use the aim locator to keep a shot focused on a target. You will learn to manipulate camera position, rotation, and aim both interactively and by editing transform attributes, so you can frame subjects precisely. Finally, you'll begin to experiment with camera attributes like focal length and depth of field, and you will use camera bookmarks to save composed shots for quick recall. For example, when you create a Camera and Aim and move the aim locator to a subject, the camera will always face that object even if you reposition the camera transform. Learning these objectives helps you move from navigation to composition: you'll move from simply inspecting models to composing images and animations that communicate mood and story. A common misconception is treating default cameras as final shots; custom cameras isolate your render setup so model work and final framing do not conflict. Practice each objective with small scenes to build muscle memory.

keyIdea.text: Build hands-on skills: create Camera and Aim rigs, adjust lens and DOF, save bookmarks, and animate camera motion.

screens.title: Default vs Custom Cameras
screens.subtitle: Understand Maya’s built-in cameras and why you create custom ones

narration.text: Maya includes default cameras named persp, top, front and side that are always present and cannot be deleted. These default cameras are designed for navigation and modeling; they are convenient for inspecting geometry and switching views quickly. However, default cameras are not ideal for final renders or cinematic shots because they are shared and may be moved during modeling. For final frames you create custom cameras which give you an independent transform and shape node you can tweak without affecting your modeling view. A custom camera can be a simple Camera, or Camera and Aim which adds an aim locator to control where the camera points. For example, when you create a Camera and Aim and move the aim locator onto a character, the camera will continually face that character even if you reposition the camera transform. A common misconception is that default cameras are sufficient for all tasks; while they work for modeling, they make it hard to lock down renderable shots because their transforms are shared. Practice creating a custom camera, look through it, and then move your model; observe how the custom camera stays isolated from viewport navigation. The core takeaway is to treat default cameras as work views and custom cameras as your render and animation tools.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Default cameras are for navigation; custom cameras are for controlled framing, rendering and animation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Default vs Custom Cameras
Core Concept

Default vs Custom Cameras

Default cameras are built into every scene for navigation. Create custom cameras when you need shots that stay fixed for renders and animation.

Why create custom cameras?
  • Lock down renderable views independently from modeling viewports.
  • Attach aim locators or rigs for precise targeting.
  • Set lens and DOF attributes per render camera.
Common mistake

Using default cameras as final shots causes accidental shifts; always make a custom camera for final composition.

Key Takeaway

Use custom cameras for rendering and animation; keep default cameras for modeling and navigation.

Quick Comparison
Default Cameras
Persistent, non-deletable views for modeling and navigation.
Custom Cameras
User-created, adjustable for lens, DOF, and animation.
Concrete example

Create a camera for a hero shot and save it as a bookmark. Continue modeling using the persp view without changing the saved shot.

screens.title: Creating a Camera and Aim
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step setup for a camera rig that points to an aim locator

narration.text: Creating a Camera and Aim rig in Maya gives you a camera transform, a shape, and a separate aim locator so the camera always points at a target. Start by choosing Create › Cameras › Camera and Aim. Maya builds two objects: the camera transform and an aim transform. To use the rig, select the camera transform in the Outliner and choose Panels › Look Through Selected so your viewport shows the camera's view. Position the aim locator near the subject you want to focus on; the camera will rotate automatically to keep that aim in frame. You can then move the camera transform with the Move or Rotate tools, or navigate interactively using Alt plus mouse buttons while looking through the camera. A typical workflow: 1) Create the rig, 2) place aim on the subject, 3) set a desired focal length in the Attribute Editor, and 4) lock or bookmark the result. A common pitfall is moving the shape node instead of the transform; always move the transform node to change world position. Concrete example: create Camera and Aim, put aim on a cube at Z=-3, set focal length to 50mm, then look through and fine-tune position. This process gives predictable targeting and makes later animation easier.

keyIdea.title: Process steps
keyIdea.text: Create Camera and Aim → Look Through Selected → position aim → adjust focal length → bookmark or keyframe.

content.html:

Create a Camera and Aim

A Camera and Aim rig keeps a target centered without complex rotation work.

1
Create › Cameras › Camera and Aim

2
Select camera › Panels › Look Through Selected
Now the viewport shows exactly what the camera sees.
3
Move aim to subject
The camera will rotate to face the aim automatically.

Set lens values and create a bookmark or keyframe if needed.
Example scenario

Create Camera and Aim, place aim on a cube at Z=-3, set focal length to 50mm for balanced perspective, and bookmark the shot as "Initial Shot".

Common mistake

Moving the shape node instead of the transform will produce unexpected results; always move the camera transform or the aim transform, not the shape.

Pro tip

Use the Outliner to select camera transforms and aim locators explicitly before editing.

Key Takeaway

Camera and Aim rigs simplify targeting so you can position the camera and let the aim locator keep the subject centered.

screens.title: Focal Length: Wide vs Telephoto
screens.subtitle: How lens values change perspective and storytelling

narration.text: Focal length is the attribute that most directly changes perspective and field of view. A short focal length like 18mm produces a wide-angle look with noticeable perspective distortion: close objects appear larger and foreground elements exaggerate depth. This is useful for establishing shots where you want to convey scale or include expansive environment. By contrast, a long focal length such as 200mm compresses depth and brings distant objects visually closer, which is ideal for close-ups or when you want to isolate a subject from its background. A balanced middle value such as 50mm often reads as natural and works well for neutral shots. When adjusting focal length in Maya, experiment with numeric values in the Camera Attributes section of the Attribute Editor. Remember that lens choice interacts with composition: a wide lens exaggerates leading lines and negative space differently than a telephoto lens. A typical misconception is thinking only focal length matters; in practice, focal length, camera distance, and framing all contribute to perceived scale. For a concrete test, render the same composition at 18mm, 50mm, and 200mm and compare how object sizes and background compression change. This will help you choose the right lens for your narrative intent.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Short focal length widens and exaggerates depth; long focal length compresses distance and isolates subjects.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Focal Length: Wide vs Telephoto
Comparison

Focal Length

Short values widen and distort; long values compress and isolate.

18mm — Wide Angle

Wide field of view, foreground exaggeration, suitable for establishing shots and dramatic perspective.

50mm — Standard

Balanced perspective that approximates a natural look, good for neutral framing and mid-shots.

200mm — Telephoto

Compressed depth, isolates subject from background, ideal for close-ups and dramatic pulls.

Practical test

Render the same scene at 18mm, 50mm and 200mm. Observe how foreground size, background compression, and perceived scale change. Use this comparison to choose the lens that supports your story.

Common misconception

Don't assume focal length alone controls perspective — camera distance and framing also affect scale and distortion.

Key Takeaway

Use focal length deliberately: wide for scale and drama, telephoto for isolation and compression.

screens.title: Depth of Field, Focus Distance & Aperture
screens.subtitle: How DOF attributes shape focus and blur

narration.text: Depth of field controls which parts of your scene are sharp and which are softly blurred. In Maya you'll often enable DOF in the renderer-specific camera attributes — for example the Arnold section — then set Focus Distance and Aperture Size to control the effect. Focus Distance is the world-space distance from the camera to the point you want in sharpest focus. Aperture Size determines how strong the blur is for out-of-focus areas: larger aperture sizes produce more blur. A practical workflow is to measure or estimate the distance to your subject, set Focus Distance accordingly, then tweak Aperture Size while rendering test frames until the foreground and background blur achieve the desired emphasis. A common beginner mistake is leaving DOF enabled without setting a correct focus distance, which results in unexpected blur. Another misconception is that DOF always needs a huge aperture to look cinematic; subtle aperture changes can produce pleasing separation without obscuring important context. For concrete practice, place three primitives along the Z-axis, enable DOF on your camera, set focus to the middle object, and increase aperture from 0.1 to 0.5 to see progressive blur. This teaches you to use DOF as a compositional tool to guide viewer attention.

keyIdea.title: DOF controls
keyIdea.text: Enable DOF, set Focus Distance to the target, and adjust Aperture Size to shape background blur and emphasis.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Depth of Field
Definition

Depth of Field

DOF controls the plane of sharp focus and the amount of blur elsewhere based on focus distance and aperture.

Focus Distance

Set this to the distance from camera to the point you want in sharp focus. Use Measure Tools if needed.

Aperture Size

Controls blur strength. Small values give subtle blur; larger values create stronger separation.

Concrete example

Create three primitives along Z: Sphere at Z=0, Cube at Z=-3, Cylinder at Z=-6. Enable DOF, set Focus Distance to the cube, then raise Aperture Size from 0.1 to 0.5 and render frames to see the background soften.

Misconception check

DOF does not replace composition. Use it to emphasize, not to hide important scene information.

Key Takeaway

Use focus distance to choose the plane of sharpness and aperture to control how much of the scene is blurred.

screens.title: Automating Camera Setup and Keyframes (Python)
screens.subtitle: A practical Maya Python snippet to create a camera, enable DOF and set keyframes

narration.text: For users who want to automate repetitive camera setup steps, Maya's Python A P I lets you create cameras, set focal length and depth of field attributes, and keyframe transforms. The provided script creates three primitives placed along the Z-axis, builds a camera with an aim, positions camera and aim, sets a focal length and enables Arnold DOF attributes, then sets keyframes at two frames and configures playback range. This pattern is useful for quickly building test scenes or creating templated camera rigs for multiple shots. When you inspect the code, notice the separation between transform and shape: we set camera transform position and then modify the shape attributes like focalLength and aiEnableDOF. A common error is trying to keyframe shape attributes when you intend to animate the camera's motion; key transforms for movement and shape attributes for optical changes. Use the example as a starting point — adjust values for your scene distances before setting focus distance. Script automation is powerful, but always verify the final shot by looking through the created camera and rendering test frames to validate DOF and focal choices.

keyIdea.title: Script purpose
keyIdea.text: Use Python to create camera rigs, set lens and DOF attributes, and key basic camera motion for rapid iteration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Camera Automation
Code Walkthrough

Automate camera setup

This example creates primitives, a camera with aim, sets focal length and DOF, and keyframes transforms for a simple animation.

Code (Maya Python)
import maya.cmds as cmds

# Create primitives
cmds.polySphere(name='sphere_obj', r=1)
cmds.move(0, 0, 0, 'sphere_obj')
cmds.polyCube(name='cube_obj', w=2, h=2, d=2)
cmds.move(0, 0, -3, 'cube_obj')
cmds.polyCylinder(name='cylinder_obj', r=1, h=3)
cmds.move(0, 0, -6, 'cylinder_obj')

# Create a camera with aim
cam_transform, cam_shape, aim_transform = cmds.camera(name='myAnimatedCamera', sa=True)

# Position camera and aim
cmds.move(0, 2, 5, cam_transform)
cmds.move(0, 0, -3, aim_transform)  # Aim at the cube

# Set focal length
cmds.setAttr(f'{cam_shape}.focalLength', 50)

# Set up Depth of Field (Arnold specific)
cmds.setAttr(f'{cam_shape}.aiEnableDOF', 1)
cmds.setAttr(f'{cam_shape}.aiFocusDistance', 5)  # Adjust based on scene
cmds.setAttr(f'{cam_shape}.aiApertureSize', 0.2)

# Keyframe camera position and rotation
cmds.currentTime(1)
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateX')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateY')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateZ')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateX')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateY')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateZ')

cmds.currentTime(120)
cmds.move(0.5, 1.5, 1, cam_transform, absolute=True)
cmds.rotate(5, -10, 0, cam_transform, relative=True)
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateX')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateY')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='translateZ')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateX')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateY')
cmds.setKeyframe(cam_transform, attribute='rotateZ')

cmds.playbackOptions(minTime=1, maxTime=120)
Notes
  • Script sets transform and shape attributes separately.
  • Verify Focus Distance based on actual scene measurements.
  • Keyframe transforms for motion and shape attributes for lens/DOF changes.
Practice

Run the snippet in a fresh scene, then open the Outliner and Look Through Selected to validate the created camera before rendering frames.

Key Takeaway

Automation speeds iteration, but always check camera view and DOF visually after running scripts.

screens.title: Using 'Look Through Selected' and Viewport Navigation
screens.subtitle: Navigate a camera view as if holding a virtual camera

narration.text: To compose and refine a shot you need to look through the camera and navigate its view. First, select the camera transform in the Outliner and choose Panels › Look Through Selected. The active viewport will switch to the camera's view so you can see exactly what it records. While looking through the camera, use Alt plus mouse buttons to orbit, dolly, and pan the view the same way you would in a perspective viewport. This interactive navigation changes the camera transform when you are looking through it, effectively letting you 'hold' and reposition the camera. Alternatively, you can move and rotate the camera transform with the Move and Rotate tools in object mode for scripted or precise edits. A frequent confusion is thinking viewport navigation modifies only the viewport; when viewing through a camera it updates the camera transform itself. For a concrete example, create Camera and Aim, Look Through Selected, then Alt-dolly forward until the sphere fills one third of the frame. Observe how both focal length and distance influence framing. Finally, lock or bookmark the shot once satisfied. This workflow ensures your composition is what actually renders and prevents accidental differences between what you see and what the render engine captures.

keyIdea.title: Practical usage
keyIdea.text: Look Through Selected turns viewport navigation into camera transform edits so you can compose shots interactively.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Look Through Selected
Process Flow

Look Through Selected & Navigation

Switch to a camera view to compose interactively, or edit transforms directly for precision.

Step

Select camera transform in Outliner then choose Panels › Look Through Selected to view the camera's perspective.

Navigation

Use Alt + Left/Middle/Right drag to orbit, pan, and dolly while looking through the camera; these actions change the camera transform.

Concrete example

Create Camera and Aim, look through it, Alt-dolly forward until the sphere fills roughly one third of the frame, then set focal length if needed and bookmark the view.

Common mistake

Expecting viewport navigation to be a temporary preview; when looking through a camera the navigation edits the camera's transform permanently unless undone.

Pro tip

Before making big changes, create a Camera Bookmark so you can return to the previous composition instantly.

Key Takeaway

Looking through a camera turns interactive navigation into precise camera placement, letting you compose like a photographer.

screens.title: Camera Bookmarks: Save and Recall Views
screens.subtitle: Fast way to store exact camera settings and jump between shots

narration.text: Camera bookmarks in Maya let you save a camera's transform and focal length so you can jump back to an exact composition instantly. To create a bookmark, select the camera, make sure you are looking through it, then go to View › Bookmarks › Edit Bookmarks and click New Bookmark. Name it clearly, for example 'Initial Shot' or 'Close-up CU', so you can recall the intent later. When a scene requires multiple angles, bookmarks save time and prevent accidental repositioning. Bookmarks store position, rotation and focal length; when you recall a bookmark your camera will be restored to those saved settings. A typical workflow is to compose several shots, save each as a named bookmark, and then iterate on lighting or animation without losing the composed views. A common misunderstanding is that bookmarks save everything about the camera; they store transform and lens values but not renderer overrides or separate animation layers. For practice, compose a wide establishing shot and save it, then switch to another camera for a different composition; return to your saved bookmark to confirm it restores the exact framing. This solid practice helps maintain consistency across renders and cutscenes.

keyIdea.title: Bookmark utility
keyIdea.text: Bookmarks save camera transform and focal length so you can quickly restore composed shots during iteration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Camera Bookmarks
Process

Create and recall bookmarks

Bookmarks let you store composed camera views to return to them quickly while iterating on a scene.

How to save

Select camera, ensure you are looking through it, then use View › Bookmarks › Edit Bookmarks › New Bookmark and give it a name.

What is saved

Bookmarks save position, rotation and focal length to restore exact framing later.

Concrete example

Compose an establishing shot, save as "Initial Shot", then create a close-up and save as "CU". Toggle between them to render both angles without re-positioning manually.

Practical tip

Name bookmarks with intent so collaborators understand the purpose of each saved view.

Key Takeaway

Bookmarks speed iteration by reliably restoring composed camera views during the creative process.

screens.title: Basic Camera Animation with Keyframes
screens.subtitle: Set keyframes on Translate and Rotate to create motion

narration.text: Animating a camera in Maya is done by setting keyframes on its transform attributes over time. Start by positioning the camera for frame one, select the camera transform, and press 's' to set a keyframe for translate and rotate attributes, or use Animate › Set Key. Move to a later frame on the Time Slider, reposition or rotate the camera for the new shot, and set another keyframe. Maya interpolates values between keys creating smooth motion. For a simple example, keyframe a wide shot at frame one, then at frame 120 move the camera closer and rotate slightly to create a smooth push-in to a character. After setting keys, open the Graph Editor to refine the animation curves: you can ease in and out or alter timing so the motion feels cinematic. A common beginner mistake is keying the camera shape rather than the transform; ensure you are animating Translate and Rotate on the camera transform node. Also remember that camera animation affects what renders; preview the animation by looking through the camera and playing the Time Slider. Practice by animating between two bookmarks or by keyframing a Camera and Aim rig so the aim remains fixed on the subject while the camera moves around it.

keyIdea.title: Animation basics
keyIdea.text: Key transforms at different frames, then refine motion in the Graph Editor to control timing and easing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Camera Animation
Process Flow

Animate with Keyframes

Set keys on Translate and Rotate, then refine motion for cinematic timing.

Set initial key

Position camera at frame 1, select the transform, and press 's' to key translate and rotate.

Set final key

Move to frame 120, adjust camera, press 's' again, then play to preview the interpolation.

Refine curves

Open the Graph Editor to adjust easing and timing for a natural camera move.

Concrete example

Keyframe a wide shot at frame 1 and a close-up at frame 120. Play the Time Slider and use the Graph Editor to ease into the close-up for a cinematic push-in.

Misconception

Animating shape attributes changes lens or DOF; animate transforms for motion and shape attributes for optical changes intentionally.

Key Takeaway

Key transforms at frames, then refine using the Graph Editor so the camera movement supports the scene rhythm.

screens.title: Composition with Cameras
screens.subtitle: Frame subjects using rules of thirds, leading lines, and negative space

narration.text: Technical camera settings matter less than how you compose the frame. Composition tools such as the rule of thirds, leading lines, and negative space help you place subjects so the shot reads clearly. The rule of thirds divides the frame into thirds; placing important elements on those lines or intersections creates balanced, pleasing shots. Leading lines guide the viewer's eye into the frame, which pairs well with depth created by focal length choices. Negative space can emphasize isolation or scale, especially when paired with a wide focal length for environmental context. In practical terms, when you set a focal length and position a camera, think about where your subject sits relative to these composition guides — then enable a bookmark or keyframe that composition. In game cinematics, the camera also defines player perspective: first-person requires careful near clipping and focal choices, while third-person cameras need safe framing for UI and action. A common mistake is focusing only on lens numbers while ignoring composition; lens and DOF are tools to enhance your framed idea, not to compensate for poor placement. End by asking: what do you want the viewer to look at first, and which camera choices will help direct that attention?

keyIdea.title: Composition focus
keyIdea.text: Use composition rules first, then choose focal length and DOF to enhance the story within the frame.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Composition with Cameras
Composition

Frame with intent

Composition determines what the viewer sees first and how they move through the image. Use it with lens choices to tell your story.

Rule of Thirds

Place focal points along grid lines or intersections for balanced emphasis.

Leading Lines

Use scene geometry to guide the eye toward the subject; lens choice affects how those lines feel.

Negative Space

Use empty space intentionally to suggest scale or isolation, especially with wide lenses.

Concrete example

For a hero-in-environment shot, use a short focal length to exaggerate scale, place the hero on an intersection, and use leading lines to pull the eye into the scene.

Misconception

Lens effects don't replace composition. Always frame deliberately before relying on DOF or focal compression to rescue a weak composition.

Key Takeaway

Compose first. Use focal length and DOF to reinforce the composition and guide viewer attention.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Working with Maya Cameras

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential camera ideas to carry forward. First, default cameras like persp and top are for navigation — use custom cameras for renderable shots to keep modeling and composition separate. Second, focal length controls perspective: short values give wide-angle distortion and scale, long values compress depth and isolate subjects. Third, depth of field uses focus distance and aperture size to decide what is sharp and what is blurred; set focus distance to the object you want crisp and adjust aperture for the amount of blur. These three concepts combine with composition and bookmarks to help you plan, save, and execute cinematic shots. Practically, create a Camera and Aim to simplify targeting, look through the camera to compose, save a bookmark for each planned shot, and use keyframes to animate motion. Keep practicing by rendering comparisons and iterating on composition choices. Which single camera choice will you test today: focal length, DOF strength, or a new camera bookmark?

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Custom cameras, focal length, and DOF are the core tools to craft cinematic 3D imagery in Maya.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
Default Cameras
Pre-existing navigation views like persp, top, front and side.
Custom Cameras
User-created cameras for controlled framing, lens and DOF adjustments.
Camera and Aim
A rig with a separate aim locator that keeps the camera pointed at a subject.
Focal Length
Short for wide-angle distortion; long for telephoto compression.
Depth of Field
Enable DOF, set focus distance and aperture to control blur and emphasis.
Bookmarks & Keyframes
Save camera views and animate Translate/Rotate over time for motion.
Summary

Treat cameras as creative tools: combine lens, DOF and composition, save shots with bookmarks, and animate with keyframes to tell visual stories.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders you can use during scene setup

narration.text: Keep these three reminders at your fingertips when working with Maya cameras. First, always separate modeling views from render cameras by creating custom cameras for your final frames. Second, choose focal length intentionally: wide for environment and drama, telephoto for isolation and compression. Third, use focus distance and aperture together to shape depth of field and guide viewer attention. Additionally, use bookmarks to save composed shots and keyframes plus the Graph Editor to refine camera motion. These practices will make your renders more consistent and your cinematic sequences clearer. When you work on a new shot, ask yourself: have I created a custom camera, set the lens and DOF to support the story, and saved a bookmark before animating? This checklist keeps iteration fast and intentional. What to Remember means create custom camera → set lens & dof → save bookmark → animate and refine curves.. In practical terms, three compact reminders you can use during scene setup. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
